news.2026-11-18-ormuz-qeshm-bahrein.titl: Hormuz: US strikes Iran's Qeshm Island after drones launched at its base in Bahrain, Kuwait targeted too
news.2026-11-18-ormuz-qeshm-bahrein.summ: On Tuesday, November 17, US fighter jets struck a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz. Washington calls it self-defense, after an Iranian drone attack on Isa Air Base in Bahrain. Kuwait says it was also targeted [1][2][3].
news.2026-11-18-ormuz-qeshm-bahrein.poin: According to a US military official, the jets used precision munitions against a missile launch facility of the Revolutionary Guards, Iran's ideological army, on Qeshm Island. Washington presents the strike as an act of "self-defense" [1][2].

Iranian media say the target was an air defense missile launcher in the Nariman area. An official from Hormozgan province, quoted by the official IRNA agency, says no residential or commercial area or infrastructure was hit [2][4].
Just before, the Revolutionary Guards said they had targeted a US radar at Isa Air Base in Bahrain with drones, in response to "repeated violations of Iranian airspace by US military drones" [2][3].

The US military command for the region (CENTCOM) says the drones were intercepted, with no damage to its equipment and no injuries. Bahrain says its air defenses stopped the attack, the second in two days [2][3].
This is the third Iranian drone operation against US facilities in Bahrain in five days [2][6]. Kuwait's army then announced that its air defenses were responding to "hostile drone attacks" [3].
Qeshm is not a new target: in early November, US officials had already mentioned "limited strikes" on the island to the Wall Street Journal, CNBC reports [7].
Key takeaway: Washington and Tehran are still avoiding a return to all-out war, but these increasingly frequent exchanges of fire threaten efforts to calm the conflict [3][4].

Qeshm is the largest island in the Strait of Hormuz, the corridor through which much of the Gulf's oil passes. Every strike in this area raises fears for the tankers crossing it. Broker XTB links Wednesday's rise in oil prices to the attacks around Qeshm and the risks to shipping [5].

For now, the market reaction remains measured. On Wednesday, November 18, Brent, Europe's benchmark oil, was trading around $94 a barrel and US WTI oil around $86 to $87 [5][8]. On November 3, after the first reported strikes on Qeshm, Brent had topped $105 [9].

The two sides tell opposite stories: Tehran says it hit a radar, while Washington and Manama say they intercepted everything. The fact that the Guards are targeting US bases in neighboring countries, Bahrain and then Kuwait, shows the conflict could spill over onto the Gulf monarchies at any moment [2][3].
news.2026-11-18-ormuz-qeshm-bahrein.forM: The price of filling up in France partly follows Brent, with a lag of a few weeks. If strikes around Hormuz multiply, oil could rise again, as in early November. For now, a barrel remains much cheaper than two weeks ago.

UK: "Brexit has not worked," admits Prime Minister Andy Burnham, three days before a summit to move closer to the EU

On Monday evening, November 16, in London, Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham acknowledged that Brexit had cost the United Kingdom more than it had brought in. He wants a much closer relationship with the EU, a few days before a summit in Brussels on Friday, November 20, without touching the single market for now [1][2].
In his speech at the Lord Mayor of London's banquet, Andy Burnham said: "The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained" [2].
He cited a sharp drop in trade with the EU and an estimated cost of 4% to 8% of British GDP [2][3].

Friday's summit in Brussels is due to seal a trade agreement on food and drink, agreements on energy and the carbon market, and a scheme allowing young people to work for a limited time on both sides of the Channel [1][2].

The limits remain in place: until the next election, Burnham is bound by his predecessor Keir Starmer's pledge not to rejoin the customs union or the single market [2], or freedom of movement [8]. His spokesperson says "the British public will have the final say" [2].

The opposition is protesting: Boris Johnson warns that voters would react if Burnham tried to bring the country back into the EU [1], and Conservative MP Alex Burghart accuses him of reopening a debate settled long ago [7].

On the rest of the world, he believes the British response to the war in Gaza has raised doubts about the country's "moral compass" [4], and he sets conditions for a future Israeli government: an end to violence and settlement building, and sufficient humanitarian aid [6].

Key takeaway: this is the first time a British head of government has said so clearly that Brexit, negotiated under Boris Johnson, is a failure [1][8]. Most economists believe it has weighed on the economy, but leaders had so far avoided reopening this painful debate [3].
Above all, the speech prepares Friday's summit. The expected agreements are concrete: fewer obstacles to selling food, links on energy and carbon, and an opening for young workers [1][2].

But he is moving cautiously. Rejoining the single market, the area where goods and services move without checks, or the customs union, which removes tariffs, remains ruled out before an election [2][8]. However, he wants to open talks on the long-term relationship right after the summit [2].

The speech also marks an open break with the past ten years of foreign policy: less investment in the Commonwealth, a relationship with China seen as incoherent, and a pledge to step up pressure on Russia to secure a ceasefire [5].

For you, this rapprochement could change concrete things: a food agreement could make it easier to sell French farm products across the Channel, and a youth scheme would reopen the door to working stays in the United Kingdom [1][2]. Nothing has been signed yet: watch what comes out of the Brussels summit on Friday, November 20 [1].

Serbia: Parliament born of the students' victory sits for the first time, Vučić moves into opposition and promises protests

On Tuesday, November 17, in Belgrade, the new Serbian Parliament met for the first time since the student movement won the snap parliamentary election of October 25. The Student List holds 140 of 250 seats. Aleksandar Vučić, now an opposition MP, promises not to block lawmakers' work but announces protests [1][2].
The Student List holds 140 of the 250 seats in Parliament, against 103 for the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), Aleksandar Vučić's right-wing party [1].
The movement defeated the SNS in the snap parliamentary election of October 25, ending Vučić's long domination of political life [1][4].
Hundreds of people gathered outside Parliament, in central Belgrade, to accompany the new student-backed MPs [1][2].
Vučić himself now sits among the opposition MPs. He says his party will not obstruct the work of Parliament, but announces that the SNS will soon hold protests [1].
The outgoing SNS government remains in place as a caretaker until a new government is approved by MPs [1].
The movement was born in November 2024, after the collapse of the canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people, and its protests continued into 2026 [1][5].

Key takeaway: Serbia is entering a delicate transition to the "post-Vučić" era, according to Bloomberg [3]. A movement born in the streets, with no traditional party behind it, must now form a government and run the country with a clear majority [1][3].

The first test is forming a government. Until it is confirmed, ministers from the SNS, the defeated party, continue to handle day-to-day business [1]. This period of forced cohabitation could slow decisions, and every appointment will be scrutinized.

The second test is the street, which is changing sides. The students won after months of anti-corruption protests triggered by the Novi Sad tragedy [1][5]. Now it is Vučić who promises to mobilize his supporters against the new majority, even though he says he does not want to block Parliament [1].
For Europe, this is a test: the election pitted a long-entrenched leader against a student movement [5]. How power changes hands, peacefully or not, will be watched closely across the Balkans.

For you, the direct effect is small, but Serbia is at the heart of the Balkans, on the EU's doorstep. A peaceful transfer of power after years of anti-corruption protests would be a strong signal for the region [1][3]. In the coming weeks, watch the choice of Prime Minister and the makeup of the new government, as well as the protests promised by Vučić [1].

Slovakia: 25,000 protest against Robert Fico, whose government discussed cooperation with Russia on the anniversary of the Velvet Revolution

On Tuesday, November 17, the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, around 25,000 people according to organizers protested in Bratislava against Prime Minister Robert Fico. The same day, his government was reviewing the revival of economic cooperation with Russia [1][2][3].
The main rally, on SNP Square in Bratislava, was organized by Progressive Slovakia, the largest opposition party, with marches in dozens of towns [1][2].
Organizers counted around 25,000 people in the capital, with no police figure. Denník N notes a smaller turnout than last year [1][3].
The whole opposition was there: liberals, Freedom and Solidarity (SaS, pro-business), Christian Democrats and the Hungarian minority. The crowd chanted "Enough of Fico!" [1][3].

Progressive Slovakia's leader, Michal Šimečka, said: "As in 1989, what unites us must be stronger than what divides us" [1]. He criticized the government for discussing cooperation with Russia on that very day [3].

A few hours earlier, the cabinet reviewed Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár's report on the Slovak-Russian economic commission that met in Moscow on October 26 [1][4]. The same day, the opposition filed a motion to have him dismissed [5].
Protesters also denounce tighter control over media and culture, restrictions on LGBT+ rights and the constitutional amendment that puts Slovak law above EU law [2].
In a video, Robert Fico praised a peaceful change of regime "that the world still envies us for" and said he hoped the opposition would not use the day to "spread hatred" [6].

Key takeaway: Robert Fico, described by AP as the most pro-Russian leader in the EU since Viktor Orbán's fall in April, is weakened, and the opposition is uniting ten months before the parliamentary election [1][12].

Fico halted military aid to Ukraine, opposes European sanctions against Moscow and refused EU guarantees for a loan to Kyiv [1]. In Moscow, Juraj Blanár made energy security his "absolute priority," mentioning more than €10 billion in possible penalties over a Russian gas contract [7].

In Parliament, the coalition of Smer, Hlas and the SNS (far right) now has only 75 sure votes out of 150, one short of a majority, after an MP defected in early November [11]. Fico says he intends to hold on until the election, set for September 25, 2027 [11][12].

On the money side, the 2027 budget, passed on October 14 by 76 MPs, forecasts a deficit of 4.94% of GDP, against 4.37% expected in 2026, far from the EU limit of 3% [8][9]. On November 16, Brussels withheld €62.5 million from a €735 million recovery plan payment [10].

Slovakia, a eurozone member, builds many cars for European brands: a country that widens its deficit and clashes with Brussels worries the whole zone. And every veto from Bratislava can block European decisions on Russia or Ukraine that France supports.

Colombia
Colombia: economy shrinks 0.8% in one quarter, dragged down by the August earthquake, on the eve of a national strike against tax reform

On Tuesday, November 17, Colombia's statistics agency DANE announced that GDP fell 0.8% in the third quarter compared with the second. Year on year, growth is only 0.5%, half what was expected. The August 10 earthquake and high interest rates are weighing on the economy, while unions and teachers are keeping their strike set for Thursday [1][2].
Between July and September, output fell 0.8% from the previous quarter, according to DANE [2]. Year on year, it grew 0.5%, against the 1% expected on average by economists surveyed by Bloomberg [1].
This is a sharp slowdown: in the second quarter, year-on-year growth reached 3.5% [4][5]. From January to September, it still stands at 2.1% [3].
Agriculture fell 6.7% year on year and industry 1.2%; only mining and quarrying grew significantly, by 7.8% [1][2].

The magnitude 7.4 earthquake of August 10, which caused serious damage in Cali and Manizales, is estimated to have taken between 0.3 and 0.8 points off growth for the quarter, according to the Bank of the Republic, the central bank [6][7].
According to the central bank, the southwestern regions and the central coffee-growing area, the hardest hit by the earthquake, saw the steepest drops in activity [8].

On the same day, November 17, Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez confirmed that the government was "definitively" dropping VAT on basic household goods, and that other revenue had to be found to make up for it [9].

Despite this setback, the teachers' union Fecode, the CUT labor federation and the Historic Pact (left) are keeping their national strike on Thursday, November 19, against the "economic rescue law" [10][11].

Key takeaway: Latin America's fourth-largest economy is stalling at the worst possible time, as President Abelardo de la Espriella seeks to pass a major tax reform to repair public finances and the street mobilizes against it [1][10].

The earthquake does not explain everything. Bloomberg also cites the high cost of credit [1], and the weekly Semana notes that the slowdown does not come only from the earthquake [12]. Banco de Bogotá adds the end of the 2026 World Cup effect, which had boosted consumption [7].

Here is the dilemma: prices are still rising. Inflation reached 6.30% year on year in October, according to DANE, far from the central bank's 2% to 4% target [13]. Cutting rates to revive activity could fuel price increases.

On the budget, the government is backing down on VAT on food, the most unpopular measure, and is even considering cutting the standard VAT rate from 19% to 18% or 17% [14]. But Fecode believes other parts of the bill threaten workers' rights and public schools [10].

For you, the direct effect is limited. But it is a clear example of the dilemma facing many emerging countries: faltering growth, prices that stay high and a state that must find money without turning the public against it [1][13]. Watch the size of Thursday's strike and what Congress does with the reform [10][9].

Hong Kong: developer New World loses more than half its value in two days after a cut-price $3.2 billion cash call

Heavily indebted Hong Kong developer New World Development wants to raise HK$24.9 billion (US$3.2 billion) by selling new shares 81.5% below its last price. Its stock plunged 40.8% on Monday, November 16, then 15.4% on Tuesday, to a record low [1][2][3].

The plan, unveiled on Sunday, November 15, offers 11 new shares for every share held, at HK$0.90 each, against HK$4.87 at the last close [1][4]. The number of shares would rise from about 2.52 billion to nearly 30.2 billion [4].

Chow Tai Fook Enterprises, the Cheng family holding company that owns about 45.3% of New World, will take up its full share and guarantees to buy any shares no one wants [2][4]. The plan still needs approval from independent shareholders [4].

The money is to be used to refinance bank loans and repay debt, including about a third for bonds and overdue interest on "perpetual" securities [2][4]. At the end of June, net debt stood at HK$126.3 billion [1].

On Monday, the stock closed at HK$2.885, down 40.76%, after an intraday low of HK$2.57 [1][3], its lowest level since its stock market listing in 1980 [5]. On Tuesday, it lost another 15.42%, to HK$2.44 [3][6].
UBS, which rates the stock a sell, says the discount and dilution "far exceed expectations" [7]. CLSA cut its price target by more than half, from HK$10 to HK$4.46 [8].
A shareholder who does not take part would see their stake diluted by 75.3% [1]. To keep up, a small investor has to put in more money: the daily The Standard puts this cost at HK$9,900 [8].

In October, the Hong Kong Airport Authority had already rescued the group by taking over the 11 Skies project, valued at $18 billion, with an option to buy 750 million New World shares, about 30%, from Chow Tai Fook for 2.25 billion [9].
Key takeaway: one of the big names in Hong Kong real estate has to ask its shareholders to pay for its survival, and the price chosen shows the scale of its difficulties [1][2].

The group is paying for the crisis in Chinese and Hong Kong real estate. In September 2024, it had announced its first annual loss in twenty years [10]. The deal is meant to cut its net debt from 68.3% to 48.3% of its equity [2].

The Cheng family is not giving up control: if no one else subscribes, its holding company would rise to 72.5% of the capital, according to Morgan Stanley. That would make it easier to exercise the option held by the Airport Authority, a public body [3][11]. Some analysts fear the opposite, that dilution will reduce the value of this option; the Authority has not commented [12].

You may own "emerging markets" or "Asia" funds that hold Hong Kong stocks. This case shows a simple rule: when a company issues many new shares at a low price, each existing share is worth less. If you ever receive "rights" on one of your shares, not responding can cost you dearly.

How it works: a rights issue

A company short of money can create new shares and offer them first to its shareholders, in proportion to what they hold: this is a "rights" issue [5]. To persuade them, it sells them below the market price. Here, 11 shares at HK$0.90 for every old one trading at 4.87 [1]. The market then calculates a "theoretical price": 12 shares together worth 4.87 + 11 × 0.90 = HK$14.77, or about HK$1.23 each, the figure cited by analysts [3]. The share price therefore drops mechanically toward that level. Shareholders who pay for their new shares keep their slice of the pie; those who do nothing see their slice shrink, here by 75.3% [1]. The bigger the discount, the surer the company is to find buyers, but the stronger the distress signal.
Precedents: cash calls and warning signs at New World
March 2, 2009

In the middle of the financial crisis, HSBC launched the largest rights issue in British history: £12.5 billion, 5 new shares for every 12 at 254 pence, 48% below Friday's price of 491.25 pence. The stock ended the day at 399 pence [14][15].
Despite the first-day drop, 96.6% of the new shares found buyers: the money did come in [16].
October 2023
After disappointing annual results, New World shares fell as much as 7.9%, to their lowest since November 2003 [17].
It was the start of a long slide: by 2024, the stock had lost about 80% from its mid-2021 peak [10].
September 2, 2024
New World announced an annual loss of up to HK$20 billion, its first in twenty years. The stock ended down 13%, at HK$6.83, its lowest in 21 years [10][18].
The losses wore down the group's cushion: two years later, it has to ask its shareholders for fresh money [1].

news.2026-11-18-senat-schumer-van-hollen: United States: Chuck Schumer says he has the votes to lead the future Democratic Senate, facing a challenge from Chris Van Hollen

On Tuesday, November 17, after a lunch of Democratic senators, Chuck Schumer said he had secured the votes to become Senate Majority Leader in January. His rival Chris Van Hollen, who has been challenging him since November 12, disputes this. The secret-ballot vote is expected in December [1][2][3].
Chris Van Hollen, a senator from Maryland, launched his challenge on Thursday, November 12: it is the first time in three decades that the post has been contested [2].
To win, a candidate needs a simple majority of Democratic senators in the next Congress, or 29 out of 56 if the Alaska race goes to the Democrats [3].
Van Hollen says he has 15 votes locked in, but only four senators and senators-elect have publicly declared for him [1][3].
According to a Data for Progress poll, 56% of Democratic-leaning voters want a new leader, and they prefer Van Hollen to Schumer [4].

Key takeaway: after their midterm election win, the Democrats will control the Senate. Their leader will decide which bills are put to a vote, and therefore the battles with Trump over his tariffs or immigration [1][3].
According to the Washington Times, most senators refuse to choose publicly, because they are afraid of opposing the powerful Schumer [3].

For you, this choice matters because the Senate can slow down or support Trump's trade policy, which weighs on European exports. A more combative leader would harden the standoff with the White House [1][3].

news.2026-11-18-italie-procedure-deficit: Italy: Brussels opens the door to an exit from the excessive deficit procedure in spring 2027, but debt will exceed Greece's

On Tuesday, November 17, European Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said Italy could exit next year the procedure that sanctions countries with excessive deficits, if its 2026 deficit stays below 3% of GDP. But the Commission also forecasts that Italy will have the highest debt in the eurozone [1][2][3].
The Commission forecasts a deficit of 2.9% of GDP in 2026, after 3.1% in 2025, then 3.5% in 2027 and 3.2% in 2028 [1][3].
The increase comes from flexibility built into EU rules to fund more defense and energy spending; Brussels will check that the entire overshoot is explained by this spending [1][3].
Public debt would reach 137.9% of GDP at the end of 2026, against 135.7% for Greece [2].
Growth for 2026 has been revised to 1%, against 0.5% forecast in May [1].
Key takeaway: exiting this procedure, which involves close monitoring by Brussels, is a long-standing goal of Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti ahead of the parliamentary election due in 2027 [1].
The 2027 budget is under discussion: parliamentary groups had until the evening of November 17 to table their amendments, including about €500 million more for healthcare [4].
Italy is the eurozone's third-largest economy. If its debt causes concern, its borrowing costs rise, and that can shake markets across the euro area, all the way to loan rates in France.

news.2026-11-18-portugal-bruxelles-crois: Portugal: Brussels raises growth forecast to 2.3% but expects deficits to return and worries about housing prices

On Tuesday, November 17, the European Commission raised its growth forecast for Portugal to 2.3% in 2026, from 1.7% previously. But it sees public finances slipping back into the red as early as 2027, unlike the government, and flags the housing crisis as a risk [1][2][3].
Brussels expects a small budget surplus of 0.1% of GDP in 2026, then deficits of 0.1% in 2027 and 0.3% in 2028; the government's 2027 budget, by contrast, forecasts a surplus [1][2].
Growth would slow to 1.9% in 2027, while the government is betting on 2.1% [1].
Inflation would reach 3.2% in 2026, driven by energy, against 2.9% according to the government [4].
In the second quarter, housing prices jumped 16.5% year on year, the biggest increase in the EU according to Eurostat [3].
Key takeaway: Portugal remains one of Europe's top performers, helped by the completion of projects funded by the European recovery plan, but this momentum is expected to fade [1].
The disagreement comes at a bad time: Parliament must vote on the 2027 budget, which is being challenged by a public sector strike planned for November 20 [5].
If you dream of moving to or investing in Portugal, soaring rents and property prices are making life there more expensive, including for French people already living there.

news.2026-11-18-bresil-senat-ajustement-: Brazil: with no deal, the Senate postpones to Wednesday the final vote on Lula's savings plan, up to 60 billion reais in 2027

On Tuesday, November 17, Brazilian Senate President Davi Alcolumbre postponed to Wednesday the vote on the last four points of the bill meant to repair public finances. Rapporteur Eduardo Braga asked for more time to reach an agreement between the government and the opposition [1][2].
The main text, rewritten by Senator Jaques Wagner, was adopted on November 12. It provides for 56 to 60 billion reais in savings in 2027, depending on the source [1][3].
The outstanding points concern the sums paid to states and municipalities, and a cap of 3 billion reais a year on certain pension payments [1].
The vote on the last amendments, known as "destaques," has been postponed to this Wednesday, November 18 [1][2].
The same day, according to The Rio Times, the dollar closed at 5.78 reais, its highest close in a year [3].
Key takeaway: Brasília must show it has its finances under control, and each postponement of the final vote feeds investors' doubts about the real [1][3].

A weak real makes imports more expensive and complicates the job of the central bank, which would like to cut rates. Hence the importance of this savings plan, expected before the vote on the 2027 budget [1][3].
Brazil sells a lot of coffee, soybeans and meat. A weak real makes these products cheaper to export, but the effect on your grocery bill remains indirect.
